q.t: From a point 20 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 45°. Find the height.
q.e: tan 45° = height/20 = 1, so height equals distance.

q.t: From a point 10 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 60°. Find the height.
q.e: height = 10 × tan 60° = 10√3.

q.t: A kite string 100 m long makes 30° with the ground. How high is the kite?
q.e: The string is the hypotenuse: height = 100 sin 30°.

q.t: A pole’s shadow is as long as the pole. Find the sun’s angle of elevation in degrees.
q.e: tan θ = height/shadow = 1.

q.t: How is the angle of depression from A to B related to the angle of elevation from B to A?
q.e: Both are measured from horizontal lines, which are parallel — so they are alternate angles.

q.t: A tower 50√3 m high is seen from a point 50 m from its foot. Find the angle of elevation in degrees.
A 6 m ladder makes 60° with the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
q.e: height = 6 sin 60° = 6 × √3/2.

q.t: From the top of a 30 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is 45°. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?
q.e: tan 45° = 30/distance = 1.

q.t: When we look up from the horizontal at an object, the angle formed is the…
q.e: Looking up from the horizontal is ‘elevation’; looking down is ‘depression’.

q.t: A 10 m pole casts a shadow 10√3 m long. Find the sun’s elevation in degrees.
Wind snaps a tree; the top touches the ground 12 m from the foot, making 30° with the ground. Find the tree’s original height.
q.e: Standing part = 12 tan 30° = 4√3; broken part = 12 ÷ cos 30° = 8√3. Total 12√3.

q.t: From a point 30 m from the foot of a tower, the angle of elevation of its top is 30°. Find the height.
A tower’s shadow is 50 m longer when the sun’s elevation is 30° than when it is 60°. Find the tower’s height.
q.e: Shadows are h√3 and h/√3. Difference h(√3 − 1/√3) = 2h/√3 = 50.

q.t: A boy 1.6 m tall stands 30 m from a tower and sees its top at 45°. Find the tower’s height.
q.e: Above his eyes the tower rises 30 tan 45° = 30 m; add his eye height.

q.t: From the top of a 75 m tower, the angle of depression of a car is 30°. How far is the car from the foot?
q.e: The angle of elevation from the car is also 30°: distance = 75/tan 30° = 75√3.

q.t: A kite flies 90 m high; its string makes 60° with the ground. Find the string’s length (assume it is straight).
Two equal poles stand on opposite sides of a 120 m road. From a point between them the angles of elevation are 60° and 30°. Find their height.
From the foot of a building, the angle of elevation of the top of a 60 m tower is 60°. From the foot of the tower, the elevation of the building’s top is 30°. Find the building’s height.
q.e: Distance = 60/√3 = 20√3. Building = 20√3 × tan 30° = 20.

q.t: From the top of a 10 m building, the angle of elevation of a tower’s top is 60° and the angle of depression of its foot is 45°. Find the tower’s height.
q.e: The 45° gives distance 10 m. Above the building the tower rises 10 tan 60° = 10√3.

q.t: From a ship’s deck 10 m above the water, the angle of elevation of a hill top is 60° and the angle of depression of its base is 30°. Find the hill’s height.
q.e: Distance = 10/tan 30° = 10√3. Above the deck: 10√3 × √3 = 30. Total 30 + 10.

q.t: A 5 m flagpole stands on a building. From a point on the ground, the elevations of the top of the flag and the top of the building are 60° and 45°. Find the building’s height.
q.e: The 45° makes distance = h. Then h + 5 = h√3, so h = 5/(√3 − 1) = 5(√3 + 1)/2.

q.t: From the top of a 100 m lighthouse, two ships on opposite sides are seen at depressions of 30° and 45°. How far apart are the ships?
q.e: Distances are 100√3 and 100 on opposite sides, so add them.

q.t: From the top of a 60 m lighthouse, two ships on the same side, in line with its foot, are seen at depressions of 45° and 60°. How far apart are they?
q.e: Distances are 60 and 60/√3 = 20√3, so the gap is 60 − 20√3.

q.t: A plane flies level at 1200√3 m. Its angle of elevation from a point on the ground changes from 60° to 30° in 10 seconds. Find its speed in km/h.
q.e: Horizontal distances are 1200√3/√3 = 1200 and 1200√3 × √3 = 3600. It covers 2400 m in 10 s, i.e. 240 m/s × 3.6.

q.t: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car coming straight towards it changes from 30° to 60° in 12 seconds. How many more seconds until it reaches the foot?
q.e: Distances are h√3 and h/√3. It covered 2h/√3 in 12 s; the remaining h/√3 is half that.

q.t: From the top of a 60 m building, the angles of depression of the top and bottom of a tower are 30° and 60°. Find the tower’s height.
q.e: Distance = 60/tan 60° = 20√3. Drop to the tower’s top = 20√3 × tan 30° = 20. Tower = 60 − 20.

q.t: A balloon at a fixed height of 100√3 m drifts with the wind. Its angle of elevation from a point changes from 60° to 30°. How far did it drift?
q.e: Horizontal distances 100√3/√3 = 100 and 100√3 × √3 = 300.

q.t: Wind snaps a tree; the top touches the ground 10 m from the foot, making 60° with the ground. Find the original height.
q.e: Standing part = 10 tan 60° = 10√3; broken part = 10 ÷ cos 60° = 20.

q.t: A pole’s shadow is 10 m longer when the sun’s elevation is 30° than when it is 45°. Find the pole’s height.
From the foot of a 40 m tower the angle of elevation of a hill top is 60°; from the foot of the hill the elevation of the tower’s top is 30°. Find the hill’s height.
q.e: Distance = 40/tan 30° = 40√3. Hill = 40√3 × tan 60° = 120.

q.t: From a point 20 m above a still lake, the angle of elevation of a cloud is 30° and the angle of depression of its reflection is 60°. Find the cloud’s height above the lake.
q.e: The reflection is as far below the water as the cloud is above. With horizontal distance d: H − 20 = d/√3 and H + 20 = d√3. Dividing: H + 20 = 3(H − 20).

q.t: Points A and B are on opposite sides of a tower, 100 m apart and in line with its foot. The angles of elevation of its top are 45° and 30°. Find its height.
The angle of elevation of a tower’s top is 30°. After walking 20 m towards it, the angle is 45°. Find its height.
The angles of elevation of a tower’s top from points 4 m and 16 m from its foot (same side, in a line) add up to 90°. Find the tower’s height.
q.e: Call the angles θ (from 16 m) and 90° − θ (from 4 m). The two right triangles then have the same angles in swapped places, so they are similar: h/4 = 16/h. So h² = 64 and h = 8.

q.t: From a point P on the ground, the elevation of the top of a 10 m building is 30°, and of the top of a flagpole on it is 45°. Find the flagpole’s length.
q.e: Distance = 10/tan 30° = 10√3. At 45°, the flag’s top is 10√3 high, so the flag is 10√3 − 10.

q.t: From the top of a 100 m lighthouse, the angle of depression of a ship changes from 30° to 45°. How far did the ship move? (Use √3 = 1.732.)
From the top of a 100 m lighthouse, the depression of a ship changes from 30° to 45° in 2 minutes. Find its speed in m/min. (Use √3 = 1.732.)
q.e: It moved 100(√3 − 1) = 73.2 m in 2 minutes.

q.t: A flagstaff of height h stands on a tower. From a point on the ground, the angles of elevation of its bottom and top are α and β. The tower’s height is…
o: h tan α/(tan β − tan α)
h tan β/(tan β − tan α)
q.e: With distance d: tower = d tan α and tower + h = d tan β. So d = h/(tan β − tan α); multiply by tan α.

q.t: From a point 40 m from a tower the elevation of its top is 30°. How much higher must it be built for the angle to become 60°?
A ladder against a wall makes 60° with the ground. Its foot is pulled 4 m further out and it now makes 30°. Find its length.
q.e: Foot distances L cos 30° and L cos 60° differ by 4: L(√3 − 1)/2 = 4, so L = 8/(√3 − 1).
